rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī identifies the “most decrepit age” as seventy-five years.
rows.anchor: نقل عن علي عليه السلام أنه قال : أرذل العمر خمس وسبعون سنة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda gives ninety years as the age meant by the phrase.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : تسعون سنة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī interprets the phrase as senility.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي : إنه الخرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers long age: senility is loss of reason, which the verse presents as the end caused by reaching decrepit age; equating them makes cause and end identical.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أولى ؛ لأن الخرف معناه زوال العقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view excludes Muslims, since long life only increases their honor with God; Rāzī supports it with the exception for believers in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: أن هذا ليس في المسلمين والمسلم لا يزداد بسبب طول العمر إلا كرامة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says a person who recites the Qurʾān will not be returned to decrepit age.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة : من قرأ القرآن لم يرد إلى أرذل العمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains “God is knowing” as knowledge of what He does to His allies and enemies.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : يريد بما صنع أولياؤه وأعداؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes both a freely acting Creator and resurrection: God first brought humans from nothing and can restore them after death.
rows.anchor: تدل على وجود إله العالم الفاعل المختار ، فهي أيضا تدل على صحة البعث والقيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation of life and death, and of childhood ignorance, adult knowledge, and old-age loss of reason, makes a second return to life and intellect possible.
rows.anchor: فلما بلغ أرذل العمر عاد إلى ما كان عليه في زمان الطفولية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After commanding expenditure, God teaches its proper measure; the believer’s balanced spending in 25:67 is the model.
rows.anchor: لما أمره بالانفاق في الآية المتقدمة علمه في هذه الآية أدب الإنفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hand bound to the neck pictures withholding so severely that one neglects oneself, family, kinship, and good works.
rows.anchor: لا تمسك عن الإنفاق بحيث تضيق على نفسك وأهلك في وجوه صلة الرحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spreading the hand fully means spending excessively until nothing remains.
rows.anchor: ولا تتوسع في الإنفاق توسعا مفرطا بحيث لا يبقى في يدك شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ethical teaching treats every trait as having blameworthy extremes; miserliness is excessive restraint and wasteful spending is excessive outlay.
rows.anchor: فالبخل إفراط في الإمساك ، والتبذير إفراط في الإنفاق وهما مذمومان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The virtuous character is the just middle course, linked to the description of the community as balanced.
rows.anchor: والخلق الفاضل هو العدل والوسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who is left blamed reproaches himself, while companions blame him for wasting all the money and exposing dependents to hardship.
rows.anchor: وأصحابه أيضا يلومونه على تضييع المال بالكلية وإبقاء الأهل والولد في الضر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says a camel is called exhausted when its travel is cut short; the verb describes driving an animal until it can no longer continue.
rows.anchor: تقول العرب للبعير : هو محسور إذا انقطع سيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural ḥusrā follows the pattern of words such as قتلى and صرعى; the verse about the returning gaze uses ḥasīr for exhaustion.
rows.anchor: وجمع الحسير حسرى مثل قتلى وصرعى

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl compares the person who spends everything to a traveler whose mount fails: needed money carries someone through the month or year as a camel carries a traveler to the next stop.
rows.anchor: المقصود تشبيه حال من أنفق كل ماله ونفقاته بمن انقطع في سفره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending the amount needed for the month leaves a person helpless midway through it, bringing blame from family and dependents for poor planning.
rows.anchor: فكذلك إذا أنفق الإنسان مقدار ما يحتاج إليه في مدة شهر بقي في وسط ذلك الشهر عاجزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Lord teaches that He nurtures and repairs the needs of those under His care, widening or narrowing provision according to what is sound and beneficial.
rows.anchor: والرب هو الذي يربي المربوب ويقوم بإصلاح مهماته ودفع حاجاته على مقدار الصلاح والصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root sense of تقدير here is constriction, as in the cited verses about a restricted provision.
rows.anchor: والقدر في اللغة التضييق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God widens provision for some and limits it for others because that distribution serves their welfare; unrestricted wealth could produce wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وإنما وسع على البعض لأن ذلك هو الصلاح لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Differences in provision arise from God’s knowledge of each person’s interest, not stinginess.
rows.anchor: فالتفاوت في أرزاق العباد ليس لأجل البخل ، بل لأجل رعاية المصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioners treated the Sleepers’ story as a test, but the answer reminds them that all divine signs are wondrous; preserving sleepers for centuries is no harder than creating and then leveling the earth.
rows.anchor: فإن آياتنا كلها عجب ، فإن من كان قادرا على تخليق السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq recounts that Quraysh sent al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ to Medina’s Jewish scholars to ask about the Prophet and three tests: the youths, the world-traveler, and the spirit.
rows.anchor: وذكر محمد بن إسحاق سبب نزول هذه القصة مشروحا

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: The Prophet said he would answer the next day without saying “if God wills”; revelation was delayed fifteen nights, Quraysh reproached him, then Sūrat al-Kahf came with the youths’ story and consolation.
rows.anchor: أخبركم بما سألتم عنه غدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kahf is a spacious cave in a mountain; a smaller cavity is called a ghār.
rows.anchor: الكهف الغار الواسع في الجبل فإذا صغر فهو الغار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that among Qurʾānic terms, al-raqīm is one of four he does not know.
rows.anchor: روى عكرمة عن ابن عباس أنه قال : كل القرآن اعلمه إلا أربعة غسلين وحنانا والأواه والرقيم

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says al-raqīm is the town from which the youths departed; al-Suddī also holds this view.
rows.anchor: زعم كعب أنها القرية التي خرجوا منها وهو قول السدي

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid interpret al-raqīm as a stone or lead tablet bearing the youths’ names and story, attached to the cave entrance.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد : الرقيم لوح من حجارة وقيل من رصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All the semanticists and grammarians cited by Rāzī say raqīm means a book, derived from marqūm, something written.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول جميع أهل المعاني والعربية قالوا الرقيم الكتاب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ describes al-raqīm as a tablet with their names and descriptions, probably named for the inscriptions.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : الرقيم لوح كان فيه أسماؤهم وصفاتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says people carved their account into the side of the mountain.
rows.anchor: وقيل الناس رقموا حديثهم نقرا في جانب الجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the youths a wonder means their episode is not astonishing beside all creation; ʿajab is a verbal noun used for the object of wonder.
rows.anchor: فإن تلك الواقعة ليست عجيبة في جانب مخلوقاتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporal إذ cannot attach to the preceding question because the Prophet and the youths were separated by a long interval; an implicit اذكر, “recall,” is understood.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز أن يكون إذ هنا متعلقا بما قبله على تقدير أم حسبت إذ أوى الفتية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths’ taking refuge means they went to the cave and made it their dwelling.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أوى الفتية في الكهف صاروا إليه وجعلوه مأواهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prayer asks for mercy from God’s stores of grace, including guidance, knowledge, patience, provision, and safety from enemies.
rows.anchor: وهي الهداية بالمعرفة والصبر والرزق والأمن من الأعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From Your presence” signals the greatness of the requested mercy, fitting God’s generosity and ample bounty.
rows.anchor: وقوله من لدنك يدل على عظمة تلك الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rashad can mean an affair endowed with right guidance so that they become guided, or that God make all their affair itself rightly guided.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير اللفظ وجهان . الأول : التقدير وهيىء لنا أمرا ذا رشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We struck upon their ears” means God put them to sleep by placing a barrier that kept awakening sounds from reaching their hearing; “barrier” is omitted from the wording.
rows.anchor: معناه أنمناهم وتقدير الكلام أنه تعالى ضرب على آذانهم حجابا يمنع

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says describing countable things with “numbered” implies many, because small numbers need no enumeration.
rows.anchor: ذكر العدد ههنا يفيد كثرة السنين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj treat adadan as an adjective of years: years having a count, with either an omitted noun or the object named by its verbal noun.
rows.anchor: نعت لسنين المعنى سنين ذات عدد أي معدودة هذا قول الفراء وقول الزجاج

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also allows adadan to be an accusative cognate object, meaning they were counted with counting.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن ينتصب على المصدر ، المعنى تعد عدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then We raised them” means God woke the youths after their sleep.
rows.anchor: يريد من بعد نومهم يعني أيقظناهم بعد نومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose particle in “so that We might know” supports Rāzī’s view that God’s acts are directed to purposes.
rows.anchor: لام الغرض فيدل على أن أفعال الله معللة بالأغراض

rows.speaker: هشام
rows.claim: Hishām argues from the apparent wording that God knows events only when they occur; Rāzī says the issue was discussed earlier and cites parallel formulations.
rows.anchor: فقال هشام : لا يعلمها إلا عند حدوثها واحتج بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the standard reading, ay is nominative as a subject and aḥṣā its predicate; the full clause is the object of divine knowledge, explaining its case.
rows.anchor: خبره وهذه الجملة بمجموعها متعلق العلم فلهذا السبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A passive reading, li-yuʿlama, avoids attributing newly acquired knowledge to God and makes the purpose that some created observers learn.
rows.anchor: وقرىء ليعلم على فعل ما لم يسم فاعله وفي هذه القراءة فائدتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the passive reading, ay would be expected in the accusative; an answer says grammatical markers can jointly identify one constituent.
rows.anchor: إنه لا يمتنع اجتماع عاملين على معمول واحد لأن العوامل النحوية علامات

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, says the two parties are successive rulers of the city and the Sleepers.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : المراد بالحزبين الملوك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the two parties as factions among the youths, divided after waking over how long they had slept; 19:19 is his evidence.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : الحزبان من هذه الفتية لأن أصحاب الكهف لما انتبهوا اختلفوا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says two Muslim groups in the Sleepers’ era disputed the length of their stay.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : إن طائفتين من المسلمين في زمان أصحاب الكهف اختلفوا

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī rejects reading aḥṣā as a comparative adjective: this pattern is not regular for derived verbs, and exceptions cannot establish a rule.
rows.anchor: قوله أحصى ليس من باب أفعل التفضيل لأن هذا البناء من غير الثلاثي المجرد ليس بقياس

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: He parses aḥṣā as a past verb and predicate; the clause is the object of naʿlam, amadan its object, and mā in limā is a verbal noun, yielding “which group counted the duration.”
rows.anchor: بل الصواب أن أحصى فعل ماض وهو خبر المبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi scholars use this episode as clear Qurʾānic evidence that saints’ extraordinary gifts are possible.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحابنا الصوفية بهذه الآية على صحة القول بالكرامات وهو استدلال ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wali may mean an active intensive: someone whose obedience continues without interruption by sin.
rows.anchor: أن يكون فعيلا مبالغة من الفاعل كالعليم والقدير فيكون معناه من توالت طاعاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, wali can be passive: someone whom God continually protects from sin and sustains in obedience.
rows.anchor: أن يكون فعيلا بمعنى مفعول كقتيل وجريح بمعنى مقتول ومجروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name wali comes from Qurʾānic descriptions of God as the ally of believers and the righteous.
rows.anchor: أن هذا الاسم مأخوذ من قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wali means near: the servant draws near through obedience and sincerity, while God draws near through mercy and bounty; this relation is sainthood.
rows.anchor: الولي هو القريب في اللغة فإذا كان العبد قريبا من حضرة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An extraordinary event accompanied by a claim may involve divinity, prophethood, sainthood, or magic and service to demons.
rows.anchor: فتلك الدعوى إما أن تكون دعوى الإلهية

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The Ashʿarī position allows marvels even for one falsely claiming divinity, citing reports about Pharaoh and the Dajjāl; their outward form already exposes the lie and prevents confusion.
rows.anchor: وجوز أصحابنا ظهور خوارق العادات على يده من غير معارضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true prophet must receive miracles; a false claimant cannot receive an unopposed miracle, and any apparent one must be met with opposition.
rows.anchor: فإن كان صادقا وجب ظهور الخوارق على يده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashʿarīs disagree about whether a saint may claim sainthood and then receive a marvel matching the claim.
rows.anchor: والقائلون بكرامات الأولياء اختلفوا في أنه هل يجوز أن يدعي الكرامات

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Ashʿarīs allow extraordinary acts by claimants to magic or demonic service, while Muʿtazilites forbid them.
rows.anchor: فعند أصحابنا يجوز ظهور خوارق العادات على يده وعند المعتزلة لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without a claim, an extraordinary event for a righteous person is a karāma; Ashʿarīs permit it, while Muʿtazilites deny it except Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī and Maḥmūd al-Khwārizmī.
rows.anchor: اتفق أصحابنا على جوازه وأنكرها المعتزلة إلا أبا الحسين البصري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An extraordinary event appearing for a wicked person disobedient to God is called istidrāj.
rows.anchor: فهذا هو المسمى بالاستدراج فهذا تفصيل الكلام في هاتين المقدمتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary’s story is another proof of saintly marvels, but Rāzī refers readers to his discussion in Āl ʿImrān.
rows.anchor: الحجة الأولى : قصة مريم عليها السلام ، وقد شرحناها في سورة آل عمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths remained alive and unharmed through 309 years of sleep, shielded from the sun; Rāzī treats this as a karāma.
rows.anchor: وبقاؤهم في النوم أحياء سالمين عن الآفات مدة ثلثمائة سنة وتسع سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some invoke the person who brought the throne before Solomon’s glance, but Rāzī identifies that person as Solomon, so the inference to a saintly wonder fails.
rows.anchor: وقد بينا أن ذلك الذي كان عنده علم من الكتاب هو سليمان فسقط هذا الاستدلال

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī objects that a prophet must have been present in that era for the extraordinary sleep to count as a prophetic miracle.
rows.anchor: لا بد من أن يكون فيهم أو في ذلك الزمان نبي يصير ذلك علما له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī replies that the sleep itself was ordinary, and its truth could not be verified until the exact sleepers were recognized after 309 years; therefore it cannot be a prophet’s miracle but is a gift to saints.
rows.anchor: فامتنع جعل هذه الواقعة معجزة لأحد من الأنبياء فلم يبق إلا أن تجعل كرامة للأولياء

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra transmits a report in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections: only three infants spoke, including Jesus and the child who vindicated the ascetic Jurayj when he was falsely accused.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The third infant in the report rejects his mother’s wish that he resemble a handsome tyrant, then wishes to resemble a falsely accused woman; he explains the man was oppressive and she innocent.
rows.anchor: وأما الصبي الآخر فإن امرأة كان معها صبي لها ترضعه إذ مر بها شاب جميل

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar transmits the Prophet’s well-known cave report: three men trapped by a rock ask God to rescue them through sincere good deeds.
rows.anchor: عن الزهري عن سالم عن ابن عمر قال

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: One man’s devoted care for elderly parents opens the rock; a second leaves his cousin and her money untouched out of fear of God; their prayers shift the stone but do not yet free them.
rows.anchor: وهذا حديث حسن صحيح متفق عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A third man preserved an absent worker’s wages, invested them until they became great wealth, and later gave the worker all of it; the rock opens and they escape.
rows.anchor: فثمرت أجره حتى كثرت منه الأموال

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A prophetic report says that an unregarded, disheveled believer may swear by God and have the oath fulfilled.
rows.anchor: رب أشعث أغبر ذي طمرين لا يؤبه له لو أقسم على الله لأبره

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib transmits from Abū Hurayra that a cow carrying a load spoke, saying it was made for plowing; the Prophet and Abū Bakr and ʿUmar affirmed belief in this report.
rows.anchor: روى سعيد بن المسيب عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A man hears a cloud instructed to water a named garden; its owner says he divides the harvest into thirds for family, the poor and traveler, and reinvestment.
rows.anchor: أن اسق حديقة فلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report about Abū Bakr says his funeral was carried to the Prophet’s tomb, the door opened, and a voice from within welcomed the beloved to the beloved.
rows.anchor: ادخلوا الحبيب إلى الحبيب

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī says that when ʿUmar warned “Sāriya, the mountain” during Friday preaching, an army messenger later reported that the soldiers heard and obeyed the call, defeating their enemy.
rows.anchor: قال علي بن أبي طالب كرم الله وجهه فكتبت تاريخ تلك الكلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed preacher calls ʿUmar’s distant sight a prophetic miracle, reasoning that ʿUmar was like the Prophet’s sight.
rows.anchor: كان ذلك معجزة لمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Nile used to stop each year until a beautiful girl was cast into it.
rows.anchor: وكان لا يجري حتى يلقى فيه جارية واحدة حسناء

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: When an earthquake struck Medina, ʿUmar struck the ground and commanded it to be still by God’s leave; it stopped and no further quake occurred there.
rows.anchor: وقعت الزلزلة في المدينة فضرب عمر الدرة على الأرض

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar wrote a command to a fire on a shard, and it went out when the shard was thrown into the flames; a separate report says ʿUthmān’s first drop of blood landed on a Qurʾānic verse after he was stabbed.
rows.anchor: أيها النيل إن كنت تجري بأمر الله فاجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Roman king’s envoy saw ʿUmar sleeping on bare earth, considered killing him, then saw two lions emerge; he later embraced Islam. Rāzī calls these reports individually transmitted.
rows.anchor: وأقول هذه الوقائع رويت بالآحاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the historically certain marvel is that ʿUmar ruled east and west with extraordinary political success despite rejecting luxury and pretension.
rows.anchor: وههنا ما هو معلوم بالتواتر وهو أنه مع بعده عن زينة الدنيا

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that ʿUthmān noticed traces of illicit looking on a visitor and called it true insight, not revelation.
rows.anchor: فقلت : أجاء الوحي بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال لا ولكن فراسة صادقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ʿUthmān was stabbed, the first drop of blood landed on the Qurʾānic words “God will suffice you against them.”
rows.anchor: فسيكفيكهم الله وهو السميع العليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the disease that later affected Jurjah al-Ghifārī’s knee began after he broke ʿUthmān’s staff over it.
rows.anchor: جهجاها الغفاري انتزع العصا من يد عثمان وكسرها على ركبته

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: After ʿAlī lawfully cut a Black man’s hand for theft, the man praised the justice that saved him from hellfire; Salman relayed this, and ʿAlī prayed and restored the hand.
rows.anchor: فسمع سلمان ذلك فأخبر به عليا فدعا الأسود ووضع يده على ساعده

rows.speaker: سفينة
rows.claim: Safīna, the Prophet’s freedman, says that after a shipwreck a lion guided him from shore when he identified himself as the Prophet’s companion.
rows.anchor: روى محمد بن المنكدر عن سفينة مولى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: ثابت
rows.claim: Thābit transmits from Anas that the staffs of Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr and another Anṣārī glowed in the dark while they walked from the Prophet, lighting each man’s way after they parted.
rows.anchor: روى ثابت عن أنس أن أسيد بن حضير ورجلا آخر من الأنصار تحدثا

rows.speaker: خالد بن الوليد
rows.claim: When Khālid found a soldier with a wineskin who claimed it held vinegar, he prayed that it become vinegar; the soldiers then found vinegar inside.
rows.anchor: اللهم اجعله خلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Khālid ibn al-Walīd ate a handful of poison while invoking God’s name and was unharmed.
rows.anchor: الواقعة المشهورة وهي أن خالد بن الوليد أكل كفا من السم

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar drove away a lion that had stopped travelers and said people are dominated by what they fear; one who fears only God should not be dominated by anything.
rows.anchor: إنما يسلط على ابن آدم ما يخافه ولو أنه لم يخف غير الله

rows.speaker: العلاء بن الحضرمي
rows.claim: A prophetic-era expedition led by al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī crossed a stretch of sea on foot after invoking God’s greatest name.
rows.anchor: دعا باسم الله الأعظم ومشوا على الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi books contain many additional reports of this kind.
rows.anchor: وفي كتب الصوفية من هذا الباب روايات متجاوزة عن الحد والحصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First rational argument: God and servant are each described as wali, and each as loving the other; when a servant obeys fully, it is fitting that God once grant the servant’s wish, as promised in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: إذا ثبت هذا فنقول : العبد إذا بلغ في الطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Second argument: denying karāma implies either God lacks the power to grant it or the believer is unworthy; both fail, since knowledge and love of God are greater gifts than bread, a tamed snake, or lion.
rows.anchor: فإن معرفة ذات الله وصفاته وأفعاله وأحكامه وأسمائه ومحبة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Third argument: the divine saying about obligatory acts followed by supererogatory devotion describes God as the beloved servant’s hearing and sight; this station exceeds feeding him or controlling an animal.
rows.anchor: ولا يزال يتقرب إلي بالنوافل حتى أحبه فإذا أحببته كنت له سمعا وبصرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fourth argument: harming God’s wali is treated like harming God, just as the Prophet’s pledge, pleasure, and harm are linked to God; feeding and visiting a believer likewise count as serving God, so small marvels are plausible.
rows.anchor: من آذى لي وليا فقد بارزني بالمحاربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fifth argument: intimacy with an earthly king can bring unusual powers; closeness to the Lord of all worlds makes saintly wonders still more plausible and spiritually insignificant by comparison.
rows.anchor: متى حصل ذلك القرب فإنه يتبعه هذه المناصب فجعل القرب أصلا والمنصب تبعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sixth argument: spirit, not body, is the agent; divine knowledge strengthens the soul as the soul animates the body, explaining why those more aware of the unseen have stronger hearts.
rows.anchor: لا شك أن المتولي للأفعال هو الروح لا البدن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlī said he removed Khaybar’s gate by divine rather than bodily strength, as his attention had turned from bodies toward the angelic realm.
rows.anchor: والله ما قلعت باب خيبر بقوة جسدانية ولكن بقوة ربانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When sustained worship makes God the servant’s hearing, sight, and hand, the servant can hear and see far away and act across difficult or distant things.
rows.anchor: فإذا صار نور جلال الله سمعا له سمع القريب والبعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seventh argument: the human spirit is not corruptible matter but kin to angelic spirits; bodily absorption makes it forget its origin and weakens its power.
rows.anchor: جوهر الروح ليس من جنس الأجسام الكائنة الفاسدة المتعرضة للتفرق والتمزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge and love of God, reduced bodily absorption, and illumination from holy celestial spirits strengthen the soul to act on worldly bodies; these acts are karāmāt.
rows.anchor: وذلك هو الكرامات ، وفيه دقيقة أخرى وهي أن مذهبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human spirits differ in strength and purity just as angels do; Gabriel is described as powerful and trusted, unlike angels whose intercession has no effect.
rows.anchor: فكذا ههنا فإذا اتفق في نفس من النفوس كونها قوية

rows.speaker: منكرو الكرامات
rows.claim: The first objection says God made an extraordinary occurrence a proof of prophethood, so allowing one for a non-prophet would separate the proof from its conclusion.
rows.anchor: أن ظهور الخارق للعادة جعله الله دليلا على النبوة

rows.speaker: منكرو الكرامات
rows.claim: The second objection appeals to the report that obligatory worship is the greatest approach to God: if those fulfilling obligations receive no marvel, those doing extra worship should receive none either.
rows.anchor: لن يتقرب المتقربون إلي بمثل أداء ما افترضت عليهم

rows.speaker: منكرو الكرامات
rows.claim: A third objection says miraculous travel contradicts the verse that describes burdensome journeys, noting that even the Prophet needed many difficult days to travel from Mecca to Medina.
rows.anchor: وتحمل أثقالكم إلى بلد لم تكونوا بالغيه إلا بشق الانفس

rows.speaker: منكرو الكرامات
rows.claim: A fourth objection asks whether a wonder-working saint’s claim to money requires evidence: accepting it without proof conflicts with the rule that a claimant must prove his case.
rows.anchor: البينة على المدعي

rows.speaker: منكرو الكرامات
rows.claim: A fifth objection says that if marvels appear for many saints, repeated exceptions become customary and undermine both miracle and karāma.
rows.anchor: فإذا كثرت الكرامات حتى خرقت العادة جرت وفقا للعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some authorities forbid a saint to claim sainthood: unlike public prophethood, knowledge of sainthood neither saves others from unbelief nor guides them, so claiming it serves ego.
rows.anchor: فقال قوم من المحققين : إن ذلك لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who permit such a claim distinguish it because an extraordinary event signals freedom from sin; alongside a prophetic claim it supports prophethood, and alongside sainthood it supports sainthood.
rows.anchor: ثم إن اقترن هذا الفعل بادعاء النبوة دل على كونه صادقا في دعوى النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They add that a prophet claims and certifies a required miracle, while a saint’s wonder is not obligatory and need not be certain or protected from opposition.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يدعي المعجزة ويقطع بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the saint professes adherence to a prophet when claiming a wonder, it becomes a miracle supporting that prophet rather than challenging his mission.
rows.anchor: صارت تلك الكرامة معجزة لذلك النبي ومؤكدة لرسالته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obligatory worship alone is more complete than supererogatory worship alone, but a saint performs both and thus exceeds one who performs only obligations.
rows.anchor: أما الولي فإنما يكون وليا إذا كان آتيا بالفرائض والنوافل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The travel verse concerns ordinary customary experience, whereas saintly marvels are rare and therefore exceptions to its general rule.
rows.anchor: محمول على المعهود المتعارف ، وكرامات الأولياء أحوال نادرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same customary-rule answer addresses the objection about evidence for a claimant.
rows.anchor: عن الشبهة الرابعة وهي التمسك بقوله عليه السلام البينة على المدعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truly obedient servants are few, so their rare marvels do not undermine the claim that such events break ordinary patterns.
rows.anchor: وإذا حصلت القلة فيهم لم يكن ما يظهر عليهم من الكرامات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Getting what one wants, whether ordinarily or extraordinarily, does not prove divine rank; it may be honor or a means of entrapment.
rows.anchor: لم يدل ذلك على كون ذلك العبد وجيها عند الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istidrāj is God’s granting a sinner’s worldly wishes, which intensifies desire and indulgence in a feedback loop and gradually increases distance from God and knowledge.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاستدراج أن يعطيه الله كل ما يريده في الدنيا ليزداد غيه وضلاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān also names this divine entrapment mكر, kayd, and imlā; Rāzī cites verses for each usage.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : المكر قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further form is destruction after apparent success, as in the people who rejoiced in their gifts and Pharaoh’s arrogant forces.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا فرحوا بما أوتوا أخذناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true saint grows more afraid when a wonder appears, suspecting entrapment; one trapped by istidrāj feels entitled, grows arrogant, and becomes secure from punishment, signaling that the gift was not a karāma.
rows.anchor: وأما صاحب الاستدراج فإنه يستأنس بذلك الذي يظهر عليه ويظن أنه إنما وجد تلك الكرامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says realized scholars have often fallen away precisely amid marvels, so they fear wonders as they fear afflictions.
rows.anchor: أكثر ما اتفق من الانقطاع عن حضرة الله إنما وقع في مقام الكرامات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First proof against delighting in a wonder: joy presumes one deserves it, though no creature has a claim upon God; joy should center on the Giver and His generosity.
rows.anchor: وهذا عين الجهل لأن الملائكة قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Second proof: a marvel is something other than God, so rejoicing in it is rejoicing in what veils a person from God.
rows.anchor: فالفرح بالكرامة فرح بغير الحق والفرح بغير الحق حجاب عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Third proof: treating one’s deeds as inherently valuable is ignorance, since every act, gratitude, and human knowledge falls short beside God’s majesty and gifts.
rows.anchor: كل طاعات الخلق في جنب جلال الله تقصير وكل شكرهم في جنب آلائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq says an accepted deed leaves the servant’s own sight: what remains in one’s view is rejected, and what vanishes is raised and accepted.
rows.anchor: فقال علامة أن الحق رفع عملك أن لا يبقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fourth proof: a wonder comes through humility; pride destroys the very quality that led to it, so its path ends in its own loss.
rows.anchor: فإذا ترفع وتجبر وتكبر بسبب تلك الكرامات فقد بطل ما به وصل إلى الكرامات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Prophet listed his merits, he concluded “no boasting”: his pride was in the Giver, not in the gifts.
rows.anchor: كان يقول في آخر كل واحد منها ولا فخر يعني لا أفتخر بهذه الكرامات
